p_simbolo_1: Castello Maresca is undoubtedly the most significant and recognisable monument of Serracapriola. This imposing medieval fortress dominates the village and the surrounding plain from above, visible from dozens of kilometres away. The castle is the defining symbol of the Serracapriola community and represents one of the most important examples of medieval military architecture in northern Puglia.
p_simbolo_2: The name "Maresca" is linked to the transformations the structure underwent over the centuries. The castle's origins most likely date back to the Norman era (11th–12th century), when the conquerors of southern Italy built a dense network of fortresses to control the territory and protect trade routes. The strategic position of the site — a naturally defended elevation with sweeping views over the Tavoliere plain — made this location ideal for a defensive structure.
p_architettura_1: The current structure of Castello Maresca is the result of centuries of modifications, expansions and restorations layered upon the original layout. Looking at the castle as a whole, the different construction phases are clearly recognisable through analysis of masonry techniques, materials used and the architectural style of decorative elements.
p_architettura_2: The oldest nucleus consists of the main tower, a polygonal keep of Norman tradition, with walls of considerable thickness in local stone. The subsequent Angevin-Aragonese additions (13th–15th centuries) transformed the simple tower into an articulated castle, with a large inner courtyard, corner towers and a perimeter wall system. The entrance portal, with its pointed arch, is a masterpiece of elegance and simplicity: decorated with geometric motifs and a heraldic coat of arms recalling the noble families who successively held the fief.
p_architettura_3: Inside, the castle's rooms feature barrel-vaulted and cross-vaulted ceilings of great architectural interest. Some halls retain traces of medieval frescoes, unfortunately partly damaged by weathering and the long period of abandonment. The main tower offers from its summit a 360-degree view of extraordinary beauty: to the east, the Tavoliere plain slopes toward the Adriatic; to the west, the Apennine ridges rise; to the north, the Gargano massif with its unmistakable Promontory silhouette; to the south, the plain opens toward Foggia.
p_famiglie: Throughout its thousand-year history, Castello Maresca has had numerous owners, each of whom contributed to shaping its appearance and function:
li_fam_1_desc: Builders of the original nucleus, during a period of widespread castle construction throughout the conquered south.
li_fam_2_desc: Under Frederick II, the castle was probably incorporated into the imperial defensive system of Capitanata, with structural reinforcement works.
li_fam_3_desc: Under Charles I of Anjou, the castle was granted as a fief to pro-French nobles. It was expanded and modernised according to Angevin military architecture standards.
li_fam_4_desc: The fief was assigned to noble families loyal to the Aragonese crown. During this period the castle reached its maximum extent and defensive strength, with the addition of round towers suited to firearms.
li_fam_5_name: De Capua family and others (16th–18th c.):
li_fam_5_desc: With the end of the Aragonese feudal system, the castle passed through various noble owners who adapted it for residential use, adding Renaissance and Baroque architectural elements.
li_fam_6_desc: It is from this family, who long held ownership of the castle in modern times, that the structure derives its current name. The Marescas made significant modifications to the residential wing, adorning some rooms with stuccos and pictorial decorations.
li_fam_7_desc: With the end of feudalism and Italian Unification, the castle experienced a long period of relative abandonment. Today it is publicly owned and restoration and enhancement works are underway or planned to make it fully accessible to the public as a museum and cultural centre.
p_leggende_1: Like every ancient castle worth its salt, Maresca is shrouded in legends and mysteries passed down orally from generation to generation. It is said that a secret underground passage connects the castle to the Church of San Leone Magno and even to the vaults of an ancient convent, allowing escape in case of siege. Some village elders tell of hearing, on stormy nights, noises and creaking from the castle's halls — attributed by the old folk to the ghost of an ancient feudal lord condemned to wander eternally for having committed acts of cruelty against his vassals.
p_leggende_2: Another deeply rooted legend tells of a hidden treasure, walled up in a secret chamber of the castle during the Napoleonic invasion, when the nobles of the time sought to safeguard precious objects and important documents. Despite several search attempts, the supposed treasure has never been found, but the legend continues to fuel the imagination of the inhabitants.
p_visita: Visits to Castello Maresca are currently organised with varying arrangements depending on cultural initiatives of the Municipality and local associations. During the summer season and on the occasion of the main festivities, guided tours are organised allowing access to the main halls and tower.
museo_p: Inside Castello Maresca, a Multimedia Museum is now active, narrating the history of the village through interactive installations, projections, virtual reconstructions and immersive digital content. An engaging journey for all ages, bringing the history of Serracapriola to life in an innovative and captivating way.
come_p: The castle is accessible on foot from the town centre, along Via Castello (about 5 minutes from Piazza Municipio). There are no significant architectural barriers for the external visit.
